utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. May I ask just for one bit of housekeeping. I wanted to make sure that yesterday's two exhibits which were Prosecution's 3/1.77 and 1.78, were in fact admitted. They were -- the necessary predicate was given and the witness in fact did address the documents. However, at the end of the session, I think because we got so involved in the other discussion, I did not see that the Chamber in fact moved them in, and I wanted to make sure that we didn't lose that particular point too far from time of seeking to move them in. And I also wanted to raise, and I must take responsibility for having come with a different -- from another Chamber where the practice was somewhat different in terms of moving into evidence. It was perhaps a bit less formal. And last week's Basrak evidence, there were several documents as well where I may have just said "I move them in" without getting a ruling on it. Again, this is something I simply have brought from another Chamber, and I must adapt to the practices of this Chamber. And if the record could so reflect that, I would ask that all of these documents officially be moved into evidence as I had indicated, and I think they had met the test. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Susan Somers. May I also regulate certain matters and start off by saying "good morning" to one and all before we go into matters in hand. I think that we're going to have a Status Conference tomorrow because I -- according to the rules of the Chamber, I don't wish to use time allotted to proceedings and testimony to matters which could be discussed in Status Conferences. The admission of these documents was regulated by a decision of the Chamber. It was ruling number three -- Chamber III brought in the ruling, and I will have to go into the matter again. I think there was a ruling by this Chamber as well which responded to the Prosecutor's request with respect to certain documents, but I can tell you now that I'm not able at this point in time to recall the situation from memory. So I'll have to look it up, and perhaps we could have a Status Conference tomorrow precisely to be able to inform you what was decided, what ruling was taken, or to discuss any outstanding matters with respect to those documents if the occasion arises and if it is necessary. And then I can also have the parties' views with respect to the calendar, our timetable. I have asked the jurists of the Chamber to contact the Kos Defence because that is our second case, our second accused, with respect to a proposition, and so I would also like to discuss that issue at a Status Conference tomorrow with all parties present, the Prosecution and the Defence. So Ms. Susan Somers, the question of documents, let's leave it for tomorrow, shall we? And also, I shall be able to tell you of the rulings that have been made and to hear Mr. Krstan Simic as well. I should just like to take advantage of this opportunity to remind the parties and to share with them one of our preoccupations, and that is the Chamber is going to make an all-out effort and do everything in its power -- and I have always said that the Chamber will exercise its authority in a comprehensive manner and in an explicative manner. Perhaps the Chamber will use its authority and put an end to a discussion. I think you will all remember that I asked the Prosecution, in presenting its evidence, that it is a long way -- that we have been discussing Omarska for a long time, and we have had a lot of repetition, and perhaps this is the right moment to say that the right road to emerging from Omarska is also a broad one, and it is a meandering -- sometimes we take the meandering roads and not the most direct route. So I should like to ask the parties, as far as is possible, to attack the questions they have directly and the issues directly. I have not intervened, as you know, in the presentation of evidence or the Defence case or Prosecution case. I always say that we have a lot of time and scope for discussion, but we must agree on this point -- on some points and take decisions. Once we have gone into discussion and made a decision, we must move more quickly. So the Chamber has been intervening at a minimum level. We have done the minimum amount of intervention, but because I have already -- I have always thought that we waste more time if we interrupt proceedings and intervene, but perhaps the Chamber will decide to intervene. So sometimes we like to let things pass instead of using up the time to intervene, but the Chamber can use its prerogative of intervening. But I should like to appeal to all parties to do our best to move ahead and to finish on time, and my recommendation is, as a bonus paterfamilias. I think that everybody of a Latin culture knows the Latin expression very well, the bonus paterfamilias, the head of the family. So on the one hand -- at one point I said, "Let's go to Omarska as soon as possible." Now I say, "Let's get away from Omarska and out of Omarska as soon as possible." But if we go to the heart of the matter, if we target the core, we will be more effective and clearer. So I am still going to try and intervene as little as possible, but I must say that the Chamber will use its prerogative to intervene when it deems necessary. Let me remind you that this Status Conference that we're scheduling for tomorrow will give us ample time to go into any other issues, but we must adhere to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and to abide by all the rulings that have been made with respect to the presentation of evidence. Perhaps we need to have a written ruling distributed. That too must be borne in mind. So without further ado, let us move ahead with the proceedings and give as much time as possible to our witnesses and their testimony, which is the most important thing. Mr. Krstan Simic, it is up to you to guide us now. You have the floor. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence calls witness Cedo Vuleta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vuleta. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are now going to read the solemn declaration handed to you by the usher. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Approach the microphone, please. Are you sitting comfortably? I hope you are. You will now, Mr. Cedo Vuleta, be answering questions put to you by Mr. Krstan Simic. Mr. Krstan Simic, your witness. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vuleta?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: As you have heard, my name is Krstan Simic, and we know each other from the conversations we have had in connection with this case. With me is Mr. Lukic, my assistant, and we shall be asking you questions concerning a period of your life and along the lines of the conversation we had prior to these proceedings. Are you ready?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Vuleta, could you give us your full name and surname?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Cedo Vuleta.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: On the 15th of July, 1958.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: In the village of Maricka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What municipality is that?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: It is the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where is your place of residence?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Srednja Maricka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What education have you had?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Secondary vocational training, the section for electricity and power.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you serve the army, and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes. Military post 762 -- 7265 in Pula.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Can you give us the dates of your military service?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: The 12th of March, 1977, until -- I don't really know the exact date when I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were you a recruit in 1990, conscript?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where were you registered in the military books?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: The Prijedor sector of the Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where were you employed, Mr. Vuleta?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I was employed in the Omarska mine from 1984.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: And what was your job?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Maintenance of the electrical system for the mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I would like to return now once again to the year 1992. Could you tell us your military assignment in the course of 1992? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: My wartime assignment was working in the Omarska mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In the course of 1992, on the basis of your compulsory military work assignment, were you mobilised?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Can you remember when your wartime assignment after being mobilised began in the Omarska mine? When did you take up your work?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but it was at the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, for us to gain a better picture, could you tell us whether the mine functioned during 1991? Was it working at that time?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: The mine was functioning during 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When did it stop functioning, if it did?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: The mine stopped functioning when the war began in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When you say "in our area," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I mean in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Let us go back to your wartime assignment and your duties within that assignment. What were in fact your duties in keeping with your wartime assignment? What did you actually have to do?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: My duties were to maintain the electrical installations in the mine, to tour the pumps in the mine to ensure that they were working properly, to -- the pump supplying the mine with drinking water, to take turns doing shifts in the kitchen where the food was being prepared, and things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When you performed your duties within the Omarska mine compound, did you have a timetable of any kind?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I worked round the clock, 24 hours, for 48 hours, and then was off for a period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, does that mean that you worked every third day?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In the mining compound, did any prisoners appear?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of May, the prisoners arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know how long they spent there?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: They stayed there until the beginning of August. I don't know the exact date. I wasn't interested in remembering it.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Could you tell us what year that was?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were you the only person with a work assignment within the iron ore mine of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you happen to recall the names of the other people who had the same work assignment and duties like you?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: There was Branko Rosic, Vinko Vuckovac, Mico Starkic, Zdravko Bjelobrk [phoen], Dragoja Maticic, and quite a number of other people as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Within the frameworks of their wartime assignment and the functioning of the system, were there any women doing that kind of work?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What jobs did the women do?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: They were cleaning ladies and women working in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What did the cleaning ladies clean?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: The cleaning ladies cleaned the premises inside the administrative building, the kitchen, and the other facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where did the cooks work?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: The cooks worked in the kitchen at the Separacija.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How far is the Separacija building from the central compound and central buildings, the hangar and the other buildings?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: The Separacija building is a little over 2 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: The women that worked in the kitchen, did they have a boss of some kind, somebody who was superior to them in the hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: The women did have their boss. His name was Dusko, but I can't remember his surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: During the time that you talked about, the end of May till the beginning of August, who was your boss? Who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: My superior was engineer Mirko Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was his function within the mine? What post did he hold?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: He was the manager of the maintenance workshops used -- where the equipment of the mines were maintained.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was he the boss of the other workers in the Omarska mine who had a work assignment in the mine at that period?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes. He was our overall boss for all those workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You mentioned Dusko in the kitchen. Was he Dusko's superior as well?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was he also the cleaning ladies' boss?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, you said that you worked one day and were off two days, that you weren't in Omarska. You worked around the clock for 24 hours and then got time off; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where did you sleep when you were on duty?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I slept in the electrical workshop where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where was this electrical workshop located?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: The workshop was located between the maintenance hall, the hall where the bulldozers were maintained, and inside where there was another workshop where the dumpers were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What building was all this in?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: It was in the -- on the pit. It was a large hall on the actual pit area.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was that building referred to as the hangar?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I forgot to ask you something, so let me go back to that. The people that had a work assignment, were any individuals amongst them from the security service of the mine?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes. There were the guards who provided security for the mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was Mr. Babic their boss too, their superior?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Let me go back to your accommodation. The room you slept in, did you have a bed to sleep on of any kind?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Very briefly, could you describe to us how you slept during those 24 hours that you were on duty?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I slept on the office table, the work table in the workshop.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you have anything to cover yourself with?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Well, I bought some foam rubber from home to sleep on and some coverings that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: During the day when you went about your business, when you did your work, whereabouts did you move?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I moved from that hall and then I went to the open pit mines where the pumping stations were located because it was my duty to inspect those pumps every day at the open pit. Then I would go to the kitchen which had a generator because there were power cuts fairly frequently. So the generator always had to be inspected to see if it was in order and to be able to be switched on so that the kitchen could go ahead with its work. Then I went to inspect the wells where the drinking water was located to ensure that there was drinking water at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vuleta.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were there any major breakdowns in the installations while you were on duty?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What were your reactions? What did you do in situations of that kind? Who helped you?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Well, I had a major breakdown at the drinking water well when the whole mine was left without any potable water. So it was my job to repair that immediately, and I asked my colleagues for assistance, who worked with me, and the manager brought the people that I asked who were there, and they helped me deal with this breakdown.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So on that occasion, two detainees worked with you. Did I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes. Pero Lezaim [phoen] and Etalic Sradine [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: As you said, you were in Omarska every third day while the camp was functioning there. Did you happen to notice any other people doing work of any kind in the camp? Were there any interrogators?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who were the interrogators?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: They were people from Banja Luka who questioned the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did they sleep in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: They would come to Omarska every day and go back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was there any security?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: There was security. The reserve formation of the police force was -- did this, and there were policemen from the Omarska Police Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How were you able to differentiate? You mentioned reserve policemen and Omarska policemen. How did you differentiate between the two?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Well, their uniforms were different. They had the old type of flannel uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: While you were going about your business, did you happen to notice any other form of security from outside perhaps?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: There was a special police force from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you notice whether that special unit had its superior officer?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes. They had their superior commanding officer too.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did they listen to him? Did they obey him?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Not very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In the police reserve force, were there any of your colleagues, workers in the Omarska mine that were mobilised, and if so, could you give us their names?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There was Momcilo Gruban, nicknamed Ckalja. Then there was Mico Hrvacanin and Marinko Hrvacanin, Predrag Petronic, and some other people whose names I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were they employees of the Omarska mine who had been mobilised into the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes. Momcilo Gruban was a mine employee.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was Mr. Gruban's occupation as a civilian when he worked in the mine?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Momcilo Gruban was a locksmith by occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you used to see him in the mine where the camp was located?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you notice what he was doing there?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: He would go to the administration building, to where the investigators were. He walked around the premises. He entered the rooms there. We would see him on the compound. He would talk to people.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: While you were there, were you able to observe who was the boss to the reserve police force from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I could notice that their boss was Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What is Mr. Meakic by occupation? What is his profession?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Zeljko Meakic was a regular police officer by occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you ever have an opportunity to see Mr. Gruban?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you ever have an opportunity to see him issuing orders to anyone?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Could Mr. Gruban, for example, order you to do something?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: It's a funny question. He had nothing to do with me. He was not in a position to order anything to any of the workers. It was only Mirko Babic who was able to issue orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were you or any of the workers who were there because of their work obligation under the orders of Zeljko Meakic?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know who Mr. Mirko Babic reported to? Who was he subordinate to?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who he reported to, but I believe it must have been to the administration of the mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know the person by the name of Miroslav Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How do you know him?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I first met him once when I was driving my motorcycle without a license, and that was the first time I met him. He fined me on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, was he patrolling in the area of your village? Would you see him there?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes. He was a policeman in Omarska, and he was in charge of the territory where I lived, so it was perfectly normal for all of us to know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How often would he come to your village on patrol?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Very often. There were very frequent patrols there.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you see him in the Omarska camp during the relevant period of time?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I saw him several times, but not for very long. I believe I saw him on three or four occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In what kind of situations would you see him?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: He would be in the administration building, he would come out of that building, walk around; and once I was able to see when he distributed some packages to the detainees, the packages that he had brought in his vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you personally ever see Mr. Kvocka issue orders to any members of the police force there?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: During those brief sightings of Mr. Kvocka, did you have an opportunity to see him beat, torture, or kill anyone?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you ever have an opportunity to see Mr. Kvocka encourage anyone to do something which would not be proper?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Kvocka throughout this period of time while you were there in Omarska and while the camp was functioning?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No. He was there for a very brief period of time, and he suddenly disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know the reason for that disappearance?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No. I was not really interested in knowing the reason why he disappeared, but I heard from my colleagues that he had been sacked, that he was harbouring his brothers-in-law in his house, and that that was the reason why he had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, what kind of food did you eat while you were on duty during those 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: We would eat in the kitchen. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When you say in the kitchen, are you referring to the kitchen which was located inside the camp, or the one which was located at the Separacija?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Well, the food was brought to the pit as well, and when I had enough time, I would also go to the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Could you tell us something about the kind of food that there was?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: At the beginning it was good; however, as time went by, its quality deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were you able to observe or did you see that you were actually getting the same kind of food as the detainees?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: The food was exactly the same. It was prepared in one in the same cauldron, except for the fact that from time to time we would bring food from home or go to a shop to buy whatever we needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How many meals did you get while you were on duty, Mr. Vuleta?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: We would get three meals.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: The three usual meals, breakfast, lunch, and dinner?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In your capacity as workers who were employed there, you knew the cooks who were at the Separacija. Was it possible for you to get more food if you wanted?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes, because we knew the personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, you said that the food deteriorated as time went by. How could you tell that it was getting worse?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: It deteriorated because of the war and the situation which exacerbated. We were surrounded. There were no supplies coming in. There were power failures. There was no longer any yeast, flour. The bread was very sour. People would bring cornbread from home because they didn't have yeast at home. They were not able to prepare the bread the usual way.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, you were in charge of maintaining electrical installations there. As far as I understand, those installations were used for the water supply as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How was the water supply organised in the mine itself or, rather, the administrative area of the mine?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: It was supplied from the same well; that is, the same well supplied the separation plant and the mine complex as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was it a well of potable, drinkable water?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When was it built?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: The well was built sometime before. I don't know exactly when, but at the time the mine itself was constructed.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was it before you were employed at the Omarska mine complex?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So that was the kind of system and the supply that you found when you came there, when you found work there?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was there any other system of water supply to the separation plant and the mine complex itself?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was that water used for drinking for the employees before these events?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes. We all drank the same kind of water.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Prior to the relevant events, were there any objections, was there any criticism as to the quality of the water?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: The water was very -- was not always of a good quality. Even before the war, there was a disease that spread at one point, and they said that it was because of the water. That is why at some point in time we used only mineral water.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: After that, was the water in the mine analysed in any way? Was it purified?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: After that, some teams of experts arrived. They conducted certain tests, analysis, but I don't know. I'm not qualified enough to tell you more about it. They must had put some chloride into the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, throughout these 20 days that you spent in the Omarska camp, did you ever have an opportunity to see bodies?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: At the very beginning of the functioning of the camp, I saw several dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where were they?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: They were located behind the kitchen building, that is, behind the restaurant of the mine, near the pit. There were some containers on the northern side of the complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Later on, did you ever see any bodies again?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes. On one more occasion, I saw one or two dead bodies near the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Could you tell us perhaps how often you would be absent from the camp itself while you were working?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Since it was a very large area - the compound itself was between 6 and 7 kilometres long - I would probably be absent for at least six or seven hours from the camp and sometimes even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: The remaining time while you were on duty, you would be in the camp?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you ever have an opportunity to see, personally, anyone beat the detainees in front of you?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you ever have an opportunity to hear about an incident involving Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I heard something about that, but I was not there on the spot. I must have been off duty at the time. That happened during the first days of the camp when detainees were being brought in. They were getting off the bus and one drunken soldier, as far as I heard from my colleagues who were there on the spot, started shooting on the column of the people there. Mr. Kvocka ran to that spot, to the column. He stopped in front of the column. He opened his shirt wide and he said, "Do not shoot. These are people here." And in this act of courage, he saved a lot of people. He saved a lot of human lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: But you didn't see that?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that. That is what I heard from people who were there on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, did you continue working in the mine once the camp was closed down?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm still working in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You're doing more or less the same job?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: "I'm still working in the mine." MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to thank Mr. Vuleta. This concludes my examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. The Prosecutor, please. I'm sorry. I apologise. Other counsel, do they have any questions for this witness? No. Cross-examination, please. Mr. Vuleta, you are now going to answer questions that will be put to you by Mr. Saxon, if I'm not mistaken. Yes. Mr. Saxon will be asking questions of you, Mr. Vuleta. Mr. Saxon, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I'm a Serb by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I just want to clarify, if I may, a few points that you made during your direct examination so that the record is clear. It's unclear to me, when you were mobilised to work at the Omarska camp in May of 1992 and began to work there to maintain the electrical system, it's unclear to me whether you worked for 24 hours and then you had a rest or whether you worked for 48 hours and then you had a rest. Could you just clarify that, please?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I worked for 24 hours, round the clock, and then I would be off duty for 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You said that you worked in the -- in, I believe, part of the hangar building, but that you would also enter the administration building. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I would enter the administration building when it was necessary to change an electric bulb or something of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would you enter the ground floor? Would you also go upstairs to the first floor?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would you ever see prisoners there in the administration building?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: The detainees in the administration building were located on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you went up to the first floor, did you ever see detainees in any of the rooms on the first floor?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No. I didn't see detainees on the first floor of the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the hangar building, did you remain on the ground floor at all times?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever see prisoners detained inside the hangar building?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever cross the area that was known as the pista, located between the administration building and the hangar?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever see prisoners there on the pista?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever enter a building that was known as the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever enter a building that was known as the "red house"?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: The "red house"? I'm not familiar with that term. I don't know about the "red house."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, the Trial Chamber has heard testimony that during the time that the camp, the Omarska camp was functioning, that there was human excrement in many parts of the camp, that the prisoners never bathed, and that they suffered from lice and from dysentery. Can you tell us, how did the camp smell when you were there?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: There were toilets in the hangar, and when workers were working there normally, they were functioning. And I think that the detainees went to the toilets as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Please listen to my question. My question was, how did the camp smell when you were there?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Well, it didn't smell nicely, but how can I explain that to you? There were no fragrances around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You said that mine stopped functioning when the war began -- the Omarska mine stopped functioning when the war began in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Was that in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. I don't remember. I know that the mine was functioning when the war was going on in Croatia. As soon as Prijedor was attacked, it stopped functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. I just want to understand something. You talked about the water supply, and at one point you talked about how you would have to go to the pits and make sure the pumps were functioning, pumping water out of the pits, but then at other times during your testimony you talked about the wells or the well that supplied drinking water for the Omarska mine. Was there just a single water system at the Omarska mine, or was there more than one water system at the Omarska mine?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: There was only one water system supply, that is, one supply system for drinking water, which is still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There was one supply system for drinking water; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was there another water system for water that was only used for the mining processes and industrial purposes at the mine?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes, there is also the water that was used for industrial purposes. That is for washing the mine equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Right. And would you agree, then, that the quality of the water in the system for drinking water at the Omarska mine was supposed to be a much higher quality than the water used in the mining processes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's because while the drinking water was for human consumption, the water used for the mining process would be used for jobs like pumping mud out of the open pits at the Omarska mine, washing trucks and machinery, and other necessary tasks around the mine; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So normally you or other workers at the Omarska mine, you would not want to drink the water intended for the mining processes, would you?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No. Nobody drank that water.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, I think it was your testimony that when you were working at the Omarska camp in 1992, you would work for 24 hours and then you would be off for 48 hours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During the times when you were not present at the Omarska camp during those 48 hours, you can't state definitively where the prisoners at the camp got their water from, can you?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's because during the times when you were not present at the Omarska camp -- or let me rephrase my question. During the times when you were not present at the Omarska camp, the prisoners may have received water from the system normally intended for the work of the mine. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Yes, Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] My learned friend is clearly leading the witness with questions that really are not grounded in the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rephrase your question, Mr. Saxon, please, to avoid leading. I think it is something that we all do. Mr. Krstan Simic has done it many times, but nevertheless, please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is it possible that during the 48 hours when you were not present at the Omarska mine, one or more of the prisoners may have received water from the system intended for the work of the Omarska mine?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Why would the prisoners use industrial water when there was water in the drinking water well? There was a breakdown once. There was no water for a while, but it was repaired during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When the drinking well broke down, when that system broke down, the only water available at the camp was industrial water; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: The water was brought in with tanks also, with cisterns. So I do not know that they drank industrial water. It would be impossible for them to drink industrial water.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If prisoners were locked up inside the Omarska mine in different rooms, in different facilities, drinking water for at least some of them would have to be brought to them; isn't that possible?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So I'll ask you again: Is it possible during the time when you were not present at the Omarska mine that someone --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My learned friend has clearly established that the man was not present, and now he's asking him to speculate on something he knows nothing about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon, what is your response to this objection? If the witness has said he wasn't there, you're asking him for an opinion, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we are at the level of fact here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I am asking for his opinion, Your Honour, that's correct. Other witnesses have provided opinions here. It was the Prosecution's understanding that Mr. Krstan Simic is representing Mr. Kvocka. We are a bit confused by the intervention of Mr. O'Sullivan, but I will move on at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, I'm sorry, I can't let that one go by because the Prosecution, if I understand it, is arguing common purpose, is arguing that all of these defendants have some responsibility for the conditions in the camp, so it seems to me fairly clear that other defendants would have an interest in the water supply, the food supply, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I stand corrected and I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that water was brought in in tanks.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you see the guards at the Omarska camp drinking this water?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you see anyone else drinking this water?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: All the men who were there drank that water.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you see all of the prisoners at the Omarska camp drinking water from the tanks that were brought in?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, help me on this. There were several thousand detainees at the Omarska camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you testify to this Court that you saw every single detainee taking a drink of water that came from this tank?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I saw them drinking. Of course I didn't count them. I couldn't see all of them. Whoever was thirsty could drink from the tank. It was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You're talking about prisoners who were outside, who have access to this tank; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, you testified that there was a special police force from Banja Luka, with a superior officer that was at the Omarska camp, and you said that they did not obey -- that the members of this special unit did not obey their superior officer very much. You also talked about the presence of reserve policemen providing security at the camp, and my question for you is: Did these reserve policemen obey their superior officer?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that Zeljko Meakic was -- I believe the word was the "boss" of the policemen who were providing security at the camp. How did you form this impression?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What did Zeljko Meakic do or say that gave you the impression that he was the commander of the policemen who were working at the camp?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Zeljko Meakic issued orders to them, telling them what to do and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it was also your testimony that you were under the authority of a man named Mirko Babic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And Mirko Babic would issue you orders?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that lines of authority or chains of command were respected at the Omarska camp when you were working there during the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that you ate your meals at the Omarska camp, and you said that the food would be brought to you where you were working in the pit, or you said if you had the time, you would go to the kitchen. When you say "to the kitchen," are you referring to the kitchen in the Separacija or the kitchen in the administration building?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I would go to the kitchen at the Separacija. Because there's confusion here. There's a restaurant at the open pit and there's a restaurant near the Separacija, as part of the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, the prisoners who were being held at the Omarska mine, they ate in the restaurant that was closer to the pit, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: They ate in the restaurant that we describe as being at the pit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You testified that the food that you ate was exactly the same as the food that the detainees ate, but you never ate with the detainees, did you?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So you really don't know exactly what the detainees ate, do you?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: The food was cooked in the same containers or cauldrons. There were no separate dishes. Everything was cooked for the soldiers, for the detainees, for us, in one and the same cauldron.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You never actually saw what was handed to a detainee to eat, did you?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I did see the cooked food being poured for them, whether it was beans or potatoes, depending on what was on the menu, and that is what the people ate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, in 1992, did you know a man named Milojica Kos?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you get to know a man named Milojica Kos while you worked at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In 1992, did you know a man named Mladjo Radic?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How did you know Mladjo Radic?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I knew Mladjo Radic from before the war. He was an active-duty policeman at the Omarska Police Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mladjo Radic at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How often would you see Mr. Radic at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I would see him when I was on duty. When I was off, I couldn't see him. So I didn't count the times I saw him. I didn't take note of that. But anyway, he was there until the end of the camp, that is, until it was closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall when the camp was closed?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. At the beginning of August, I think. This wasn't something that interested me too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So just to be clear, whenever you were there working at the Omarska mine or present at the camp, you would see Mladjo Radic present as well?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Not necessarily. It depended on the shifts, when our duty hours coincided. But anyway, I would see him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mladjo Radic at the Omarska camp at night?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where would you see Mladjo Radic at night?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I would see him in front of the administration building where the generators were, which I would switch on when there was a power failure, and they provided the fuel for me to pour into the generator.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What would Mr. Radic be doing on the occasions when you saw him at the camp?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I would mostly see Mr. Radic in the administration building, inside. He would come out. He would walk around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You said he would walk around. Where would he walk around?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Around the administration building near the pista, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would he be armed?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: He was armed with a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How would Mr. Radic be dressed on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: He was dressed in a regular blue police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How did Mladjo Radic treat the guards at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I don't know. I think he was quite correct with them. I didn't really watch to see how Mladjo was behaving. I saw that there were no incidents of any kind. I didn't see him act arrogantly in relation to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever speak with Mr. Radic at the Omarska camp during 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I spoke to Mladjo about our work. When he would say that I needed to switch on the generator, I would do that. So our conversation didn't go beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So Mr. Radic would ask you to switch on the generator for electrical power?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes, for the lighting. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would any of the guards who worked at the camp ask you to do that, or was it a small group of guards, Mr. Radic and some other people?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I remember Radic telling me once. There was a power failure, and he told me the generator needed to be turned on. I did that, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. 1992, did you know a man named Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: 1992, did you know a man named Dragoljub Prcac?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How did you know Mr. Prcac?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Prcac through my colleagues. I never met with him personally. People would say to me, "That is Dragoljub Prcac, an older man." I never saw him before the camp. He worked somewhere; I don't know where. I would see him, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How often would you see Mr. Prcac at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Well, frequently -- not very frequently, actually. He was in the office, in the administration building. I saw him a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall when you saw him there, during the day or during the night, or both?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I only saw him a couple of times during the day. I didn't see him during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall approximately when was the first time that you saw Dragoljub Prcac at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know the date. I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How did Dragoljub Prcac treat the guards at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Dragoljub Prcac acted in a very nice way. He's a good and fine man, as far as I was able to see. I never noticed anything indecent or incorrect about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How did the guards at the Omarska camp respond or act towards Dragoljub Prcac?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I don't know that. I have no idea, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever speak with Mr. Prcac at the Omarska camp in 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, did you ever see prisoners with visible injuries at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever see prisoners being beaten or otherwise mistreated at the camp?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I saw that only when they went to eat. Some guards would slap them, or they would put their leg in front of them to trip them up, or they would sometimes kick them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever see anyone intervene to stop this mistreatment of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw Mr. Gruban, who would not allow the men to be hurt or mistreated or harassed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you can help us, please, how would Mr. Gruban intervene to stop mistreatment or harassment of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: He would simply cry out, "Don't do that. Leave the men alone. Let them eat in peace."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gruban --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon, I'm sorry for interrupting you. If possible, perhaps instead of using words "mistreatment," "maltreatment," perhaps we could use the word "conduct" or "behaviour," because we're here to make the conclusion as to the kind of conduct. Having made that interruption, I think we should have our break now, a half-hour break. I leave it with you to think about it because as you know, it is up to us to conclude whether the treatment was bad or not. If you say to a witness, "Did you see somebody mistreating somebody," this is another way of putting the question, so pay attention to that, please. And I will now ask the usher to accompany the witness out, and then we'll have our half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now have a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Saxon, according to my calculations, you still have a quarter of an hour, and, of course, you can always finish before that, but please continue. Your witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I will do my utmost to finish as quickly as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, before the break, you mentioned an incident that you witnessed where you saw some guards slapping some prisoners in the Omarska camp, slapping them or kicking them, and you said that Mr. Gruban intervened and he said, "Don't do that. Leave the men alone. Let them eat in peace." MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection. Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Mr. Vuleta just said that he saw this on one occasion. My learned friend has used the expression "several times."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at the English translation. There may be a translation problem. My question clearly referred to "an incident." That's all I'm referring to. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] The interpretation we got was "several times." I apologise. That was a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. At any rate, please continue, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, when Mr. Gruban said this to the guards on that occasion, how did the guards respond, if at all?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: The guards didn't obey him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you see Mladjo Radic present on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, I'd like to move on to another topic now. During the summer of 1992, when you were working at the Omarska camp, you were also given the task of keeping certain records regarding the prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No records as far as the prisoners were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to discuss a document with you, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has distributed a document that's been marked as Exhibit 3/1.79, and if a copy of that document could be given to the Judges and a copy placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we received this document several minutes ago in English, but I see that it is a text taken from the magazine Ljiljan, which is a newspaper put out by the SDA party, and I don't know why the witness is being asked to comment on a text taken from a newspaper and in English at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document does summarise an article that was published in Sarajevo by a journal known as Ljiljan. This article mentions this witness by name and that is why I would like to put this article or the paragraph concerning this witness to the witness. It is true that the document is in English. That's because it was provided to us not in the original but by the foreign broadcasting information or FBIS, which is a news service which provides information in English. We do have interpreters here, obviously, and I would like to read the pertinent sentences to this witness and ask him to comment on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned colleague acknowledges that it is a newspaper article, and I say again that that is the newspaper, the organ of the SDA party. And my learned colleague says that he hasn't got the authentic version, the original version of the text. We do not have the Serbo-Croatian or, rather, the Bosnian version for the witness to be able to read the entire text. You can't look at a document partially. It is a newspaper article extracted. We don't know if it was published at all. We don't know what it is, when it appeared, or anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think that as you yourself said, Mr. Simic, it was a newspaper of the SDA, but now you say you don't know what the document actually is. I think that the Prosecutor is going to ask the witness whether he knew about this article or not, whether it is familiar to him or not. So let him go ahead with the question and we'll hear the answer. Mr. Prosecutor, ask the question whether the witness is familiar with the article and then go ahead with your question. You will -- the witness will be following the interpretation of the text, and then the other party will be free to ask questions themselves. If possible, Mr. Prosecutor, could you give instructions for the document to be placed on the ELMO so that the interpreters can see the document on the ELMO and can therefore perform their task.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Usher, could you please place page 3 of this document on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you see, Mr. Vuleta, in the middle of the large paragraph that is presented on the ELMO your name appears. Can you see the name there, "Cedo Vuleta"?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm simply going to read the sentence before your name and the sentence that includes your name, and I'd simply like to ask you to comment on what the article says. The sentence before your name says the following: "It will hardly ever be learned how many people were slaughtered in that facility because no one ever returned from there. Nevertheless, inmates claim that a certain Cedo Vuleta, an electrician who performed the duty of records officer, could help a great deal in learning the number of people executed in the entire mine, as well as Vlado Kobat, the driver who took the dead and half-living bodies to the abandoned pit of the mine or even to the neighbouring Tomasica mine."

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I never kept any records.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The title of this article which is by a man named Zlatko Hodzic is entitled "The Serbs Repeated Auschwitz: The Burning of Camp Inmates in an Ore-drying Furnace," and the date of the article is 7 February, 1996. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] In the area of Prijedor-Banja Luka-Ljubija, furnaces exist in Zenica, Smederevo, Jesenice, and it is only this observation which speaks of the fact that this is not a serious article, it's not a serious text. There are no furnaces in that particular area, in Prijedor and the surrounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, objection rejected. The witness was asked; he has already answered. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to move on now. Yes, the document may be removed, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, this Trial Chamber has heard evidence that bodies of prisoners who died at Omarska were removed from the camp. In addition, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence that a number of bodies of persons who died at Omarska have been found in a mass grave in the village of Kevljani. Now, you knew, didn't you, that Kevljani was one of the burial sites for prisoners who died at the Omarska camp. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection, objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] That phrase, "you knew," is that not a leading question, Your Honours, indicating the answer? It is extremely leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, I'm not a specialist in languages, linguistics, but I do know that in the English language, when people want to know something or are asking something, are asking a question and then they put the "did you" phrase at the end, that makes it a question. So I am not able to correct the Prosecutor. Please continue. The witness is going to answer anyway, Mr. Krstan Simic. Don't worry. The witness will answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, you knew that Kevljani was one of the burial sites for prisoners who died at the Omarska camp, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I did not know where the dead bodies were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In fact, on a number of occasions, you helped to deposit bodies of prisoners at Kevljani, did you not?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was done with the bodies that you saw lying inside the Omarska camp? You've told us that you saw bodies, I think on more than one occasion. What was done with those bodies?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: They were taken away somewhere. I didn't take them away. I don't know. How should I know? I was doing my job. I had nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who took those bodies away?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: There were people who transported them. I was not authorised to drive them off or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who transported the bodies away from the camp? Who drove them off?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: There were drivers, Mico Starkic and Pero Mrdza. Vlado Kobas was also a driver. He drove a vehicle. But who actually drove, I don't know. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What kind of vehicle was used to take the dead bodies out of the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: The mine had a small vehicle which we called a Tamic. It was a TAM van, yellow. All the mine's vehicle were yellow, and the workshop had that particular vehicle at its disposal for its affairs around the mine compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How many times did you see bodies being transported in that yellow TAM truck?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I did not see that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How do you know that the bodies were taken away in the TAM truck? That's what you just testified to.

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: As the vehicle existed, that was the only vehicle that existed. So nobody could have carried the bodies on their backs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned certain drivers, Mico Starkic, someone else's name I can't see on the transcript. Who told the drivers to take these bodies outside of the camp? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] The witness has said he did not see the bodies being taken away. He said a yellow vehicle existed because that was the only vehicle that existed in the compound, but having not had an opportunity to see it, he didn't know who gave that particular instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, that is not good logic. Objection rejected. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, would you like some water?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Yes, I would like some water, some brandy too, if you have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I had some, I would give you some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But not now. Not now. [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, who told the drivers to take these bodies out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May I have the Court's indulgence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, when trucks or vehicles entered or exited the Omarska camp during the summer of 1992, did they have to have some kind of authorisation to enter and exit?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I have no idea whether they did or didn't. I wasn't interested in that at all. I was just an electrician. I was not a guard. I was not a driver or an administrative worker.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. We're now going to give the floor to Mr. Simic for any additional questions, after which I shall give the floor to the other Defence counsel if they have any questions in the cross-examination, but Mr. Simic is first. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have just a few questions related to one particular topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, when you spoke about industrial water and drinking water, what was the system used to bring the drinking water in?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Drinking water came from the drinking-water well.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where did it flow out?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: In the bathrooms. There were taps in the bathrooms, in the kitchen, in the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What about the hangar? Were there taps in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes, there were taps in the hangar as well. And that same water was in the toilets as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What about in the open space on the pista? Were there any water taps anywhere there?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: I think there were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What about the industrial water? Which taps did that come out of?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Industrial water, there was a rinsing area with large pumps and large hoses where the installations and mine equipment was washed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were these pipes screwed on to special taps?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So industrial water did not flow through the same pipes and taps as the drinking water; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes. That other water came out in this special washing area for the mining equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Could that water come out anywhere so that it could be used as drinking water?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Well, no. Not even cattle could drink that water, let alone men.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: My learned colleague asked you that when you were off the two days you were off, could the water system be changed at all, the water supply system? Could it be altered in any way?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Well, how could it be changed? No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My objection is simply I don't think that is a correct rephrasing of my question to this witness. I believe I asked this witness when the witness was not at the Omarska camp, could prisoners have received water that did not come from the potable water system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, can you reformulate your question? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I will continue on from the formulation made by my learned colleague and ask the witness the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When you were absent, was there any possibility of any other water being passed through the existing system?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: And finally, let me ask you this: Did Zeljko Meakic, the chief of the police station, or anybody else from this police station department, could they in any way influence the waterwork system, the water supply system, the quality of the water, or anything else of that kind?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: No. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The Defence counsel for Mr. Kos, Zigic, Radic, Prcac, any questions? No questions, I see. Mr. Stojanovic, you have no questions either. Very well. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vuleta. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to just make sure that I understood everything you said. First when you were answering the Prosecutor you said that you did not see in Omarska anybody beating the detainees. Did your work give you enough chance to walk around and to see every part of the camp?

utterances.speaker: CEDO VULETA
